column1: Ask an A.I. one simple question.
Will it rain in my village tomorrow?
Before it reads your question, the machine chops it into pieces.
In English... just eight.
Now ask it in Hindi.
On DeepSeek, the famous Chinese A.I.... eighteen.
More than double.
Marathi, twenty.
Telugu, twenty-five.
And in those two, it even cuts some of your letters in half.
So can India build an A.I. of its own?
One that speaks your language best?
Here's a clue for you.
Ask it in Chinese.
Seven pieces.
Fewer than English.
You see what's going on?
A machine speaks best in the language of the people who built it.
And it's not just pride.
Your apps pay these machines by the piece.
More pieces means a bigger bill, and a slower answer for you.
Now think back to last November.
Chat G.P.T.'s paid plan, called Go, became free in India for a whole year.
Maybe you signed up too.
OpenAI says India is now one of its biggest markets.
For the first people who signed up, that free year runs out... about now.
So when yours ends, whose machine will you be talking to?
One built in America?
One built in China?
Or one built here?
To see why India doesn't have its own yet, you have to go back to one Monday.
The twenty-seventh of January, twenty twenty-five.
A small Chinese lab called DeepSeek has just put out a free A.I.
By that Monday, it's beaten Chat G.P.T. in downloads on Apple's App Store in America.
